name: Mustache shield (1876)

lead: Moustache guards were Victorian devices that held the moustache back from drink and food. The best-known form is the moustache cup, which has a semicircular ledge with a half-moon opening that lets liquid through while keeping the moustache dry.[1]
The appearance payoff was keeping an elaborately waxed moustache clean and in place; steam could melt the wax into the cup and drinks could stain the hair.[1]

paras: The guard sat in the cup or attached to the drinking vessel; a moustache spoon (1904) served for soup in Edwardian England.[2]
No known health risks; the items are antique and collectible.

chain: Guard keeps moustache out of liquid

angle.text: It protects a styled moustache during meals and drinks so the shape and cleanliness survive.

lead: A moustache shield or guard is a device that keeps a moustache out of food and drink. Wikipedia credits British potter Harvey Adams, born 1835, with inventing the moustache cup in the 1870s.[1]

The need arose from the moustache's popularity: by the 1860s moustaches were wildly popular, and enlisted British soldiers were barred from shaving the upper lip until 1916.[2] Waxed moustaches suffered from steam and staining, and potteries across Europe such as Meissen, Royal Crown Derby and Limoges made cups. Fashion faded in the 1920s and 1930s, and the cups are now collectible.[1]

paras: Harvey Adams is generally acknowledged as inventor of the moustache cup in the 1870s.[1] The semicircular ledge or guard has a half-moon opening for liquid.[1] The idea reached America, where English-looking marks were common.[1]

timeline.event: Moustaches become wildly popular in Britain.[2]
Harvey Adams invents the moustache cup.[1]
